metadata.chapter_title: Linear Inequalities, Simultaneous Equations, and Coordinate Geometry
metadata.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations: Substitution and Elimination
metadata.vcaa_description: Solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables; interpret solutions graphically and apply to real-world contexts.
metadata.target_mastery: Solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations graphically, by substitution, and by elimination, and model break-even and mixture problems.

key_vocabulary.definition: A system of two or more linear equations in the same variables that must be satisfied at the same time.
The coordinate pair $(x, y)$ where the graphs of two linear equations cross, representing the unique simultaneous solution to both equations.
An algebraic method where one variable is expressed in terms of the other from one equation and substituted into the second equation.
An algebraic method where equations are added or subtracted (after multiplying by suitable constants if needed) to eliminate one variable.

theory.title: Graphical Interpretation and the Method of Substitution
theory.explanation: Geometrically, each linear equation in two variables represents a straight line in the Cartesian plane. Solving a pair of simultaneous equations finds the point of intersection $(x, y)$ that lies on both lines. The substitution method is most efficient when at least one equationalready has $x$ or $y$ isolated as the subject (e.g. $y = 3x - 2$): replace that variable in the other equation with its algebraic expression to obtain a single equation in one unknown.
theory.formula_latex: \begin{cases} y = mx + c \\ ax + by = d \end{cases} \implies ax + b(mx + c) = d
theory.callout_title: Use Brackets When Substituting an Expression
theory.callout_rule: When substituting $y = 2x - 5$ into $3x - 4y = 10$, always enclose the expression in brackets: $3x - 4(2x - 5) = 10$, so that $-4$ multiplies both $2x$ and $-5$.

theory.title: The Method of Elimination
theory.explanation: When both simultaneous equations are written in standard form $ax + by = c$, the elimination method is usually faster. If one variable has coefficients of equal magnitude in both equations, add the equations (when the signs are opposite, such as $+3y$ and $-3y$) or subtract the equations (when the signs are the same, such as $+2x$ and $+2x$). If neither variable has matching coefficient magnitudes, multiply one or both equations by constants first to create matching coefficients.
theory.formula_latex: \begin{cases} a_1 x + b y = c_1 \\ a_2 x - b y = c_2 \end{cases} \xrightarrow{\text{Add (1) + (2)}} (a_1 + a_2)x = c_1 + c_2
theory.callout_title: Same Signs Subtract, Opposite Signs Add
theory.callout_rule: To eliminate a variable with coefficients $+4y$ and $-4y$ (opposite signs), ADD the two equations. To eliminate $+4y$ and $+4y$ (same signs), SUBTRACT one equation from the other.

theory.title: Parallel Lines, Coincident Lines, and Break-Even Modelling
theory.explanation: Two lines in a plane can intersect at a single point (unique solution, when gradients $m_1 \neq m_2$), be parallel and distinct (no solution, when $m_1 = m_2$ and $c_1 \neq c_2$), or be the exact same line (infinitely many solutions, when $m_1 = m_2$ and $c_1 = c_2$). In business modelling, solving the cost equation $C = F + vx$ simultaneously with the revenue equation $R = px$ finds the break-even point where revenue equals cost ($R = C$).
theory.formula_latex: \text{Break-even: } R(x) = C(x) \iff px = F + vx \implies x = \frac{F}{p - v}
theory.callout_title: Always Define Both Variables and Check Your Solution in Both Equations
theory.callout_rule: In word problems, start by writing 'Let $x$ be ... and let $y$ be ...' with units. Once you find $(x, y)$, substitute both values into BOTH original equations to guarantee zero arithmetic errors.

worked_examples.title: Modelling with Simultaneous Equations
worked_examples.problem: At a Melbourne bakery, $3$ meat pies and $2$ coffees cost $\$23$, while $4$ meat pies and $3$ coffees cost $\$32$. Find the price of one meat pie and one coffee.

steps.thinking: Define variables: let $p$ be the price of a meat pie ($\$$) and $c$ be the price of a coffee ($\$$). Form two simultaneous equations.
Multiply (1) by $3$ and (2) by $2$ so both have $+6c$, then subtract $(2')$ from $(1')$.

now_you_try.problem: At a cinema, $2$ adult tickets and $3$ child tickets cost $\$69$, while $3$ adult tickets and $2$ child tickets cost $\$76$. Find the cost of an adult ticket ($a$) and a child ticket ($c$).
now_you_try.hint: Set up $2a + 3c = 69$ and $3a + 2c = 76$, then eliminate one variable.

common_misconceptions.title: Adding Instead of Subtracting When Eliminating Terms with the Same Sign
common_misconceptions.misconception: Adding $2x + 3y = 13$ and $5x + 3y = 22$ to get $7x = 35$, forgetting that $+3y + (+3y) = +6y \neq 0$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: When the coefficients of the variable to be eliminated have the SAME sign (both $+3y$ or both $-3y$), you must SUBTRACT one equation from the other so that $3y - 3y = 0$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: If $x = 5$ (from the incorrect addition), $2(5) + 3y = 13 \implies y = 1$, which fails in the second equation: $5(5) + 3(1) = 28 \neq 22$.

common_misconceptions.title: Forgetting to Multiply the Right-Hand Side Constant When Scaling an Equation
common_misconceptions.misconception: Multiplying the left-hand side of $2x + 3y = 7$ by $4$ to get $8x + 12y = 7$ instead of $8x + 12y = 28$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: To preserve equality, every term on BOTH sides of the equation—including the constant on the right-hand side—must be multiplied by the scaling factor.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the simultaneous equations $y = 4x - 7$ and $2x + y = 11$ using substitution.
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $y = 4x - 7$ into $2x + y = 11$: $2x + (4x - 7) = 11 \implies 6x = 18 \implies x = 3$.
Substitute $x = 3$ into $y = 4x - 7$: $y = 4(3) - 7 = 5$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the simultaneous equations $4x + 3y = 18$ and $2x - 3y = 0$ using elimination.
step_by_step_solution: Add the two equations to eliminate $y$: $(4x + 2x) + (3y - 3y) = 18 + 0 \implies 6x = 18 \implies x = 3$.
Substitute $x = 3$ into $2x - 3y = 0$: $6 - 3y = 0 \implies y = 2$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the simultaneous equations $5x + 2y = 11$ and $3x + 2y = 9$.
step_by_step_solution: Subtract the second equation from the first: $(5x - 3x) + (2y - 2y) = 11 - 9 \implies 2x = 2 \implies x = 1$.
Substitute $x = 1$ into $3x + 2y = 9$: $3 + 2y = 9 \implies 2y = 6 \implies y = 3$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Solve the simultaneous equations $4x - 3y = 18$ and $3x + 5y = -1$.
step_by_step_solution: Multiply the first equation by $5$ ($20x - 15y = 90$) and the second equation by $3$ ($9x + 15y = -3$).
Add the scaled equations: $29x = 87 \implies x = 3$.
Substitute $x = 3$ into $3x + 5y = -1$: $9 + 5y = -1 \implies 5y = -10 \implies y = -2$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A Bendigo craftsperson makes wooden chopping boards. Setup costs are $\$360$ plus $\$12$ in timber per board ($C = 12n + 360$). Each board sells for $\$30$ ($R = 30n$). Find the break-even number of boards $n$ and the revenue at the break-even point.
step_by_step_solution: At break-even, $R = C$: $30n = 12n + 360$.
Subtract $12n$: $18n = 360 \implies n = 20\text{ boards}$.
Break-even revenue $= 30 \times 20 = \$600$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A rectangle has a perimeter of $46\text{ cm}$. Its length $L$ is $5\text{ cm}$ greater than twice its width $W$. Set up and solve a pair of simultaneous equations to find $L$ and $W$.
step_by_step_solution: From the perimeter, $2L + 2W = 46 \implies L + W = 23$. From the length relation, $L = 2W + 5$.
Substitute $L = 2W + 5$ into $L + W = 23$: $(2W + 5) + W = 23 \implies 3W = 18 \implies W = 6\text{ cm}$.
Then $L = 2(6) + 5 = 17\text{ cm}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A chemist needs $100\text{ mL}$ of a $28\%$ acid solution by mixing $x\text{ mL}$ of a $20\%$ acid solution with $y\text{ mL}$ of a $40\%$ acid solution. Write and solve simultaneous equations to find $x$ and $y$.
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: $x = 60\text{ mL}$ of $20\%$ solution and $y = 40\text{ mL}$ of $40\%$ solution
step_by_step_solution: Total volume equation: $x + y = 100$. Pure acid volume equation: $0.20x + 0.40y = 0.28(100) = 28$ (or $2x + 4y = 280$).
Substitute $y = 100 - x$ into $2x + 4y = 280$: $2x + 4(100 - x) = 280 \implies -2x = -120 \implies x = 60\text{ mL}$.
Then $y = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ mL}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A river boat on the Murray River travels $36\text{ km}$ downstream in $2\text{ hours}$ and returns the same $36\text{ km}$ upstream in $3\text{ hours}$. Find the speed of the boat in still water ($b\text{ km/h}$) and the speed of the river current ($c\text{ km/h}$).
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: Boat speed $15\text{ km/h}$; current speed $3\text{ km/h}$
step_by_step_solution: Downstream speed is $b + c = \frac{36}{2} = 18\text{ km/h}$; upstream speed is $b - c = \frac{36}{3} = 12\text{ km/h}$.
Add the two equations: $2b = 30 \implies b = 15\text{ km/h}$.
Substitute $b = 15$: $15 + c = 18 \implies c = 3\text{ km/h}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Explain both algebraically and geometrically why the simultaneous system $2x - y = 4$ and $4x - 2y = 10$ has no solution.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Multiplying the first equation by $2$ gives $4x - 2y = 8 \neq 10$; geometrically both lines have gradient $m = 2$ but different $y$-intercepts ($-4$ and $-5$), so they are parallel and never intersect
step_by_step_solution: Algebraically, multiplying $2x - y = 4$ by $2$ gives $4x - 2y = 8$, which contradicts $4x - 2y = 10$ (subtracting gives $0 = -2$, a contradiction).
Geometrically, rearranging into gradient-intercept form gives $y = 2x - 4$ and $y = 2x - 5$: parallel distinct lines with gradient $2$ that never intersect.

reasoning_and_communication.question: For the system $3x + ky = 6$ and $6x + 8y = 12$, find the value of $k$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and explain what happens geometrically for this value of $k$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: $k = 4$; the two equations represent the exact same (coincident) straight line
step_by_step_solution: Notice that the $x$-coefficient and constant in $6x + 8y = 12$ are exactly twice those in $3x + ky = 6$.
For the two equations to be identical multiples of each other, $2k = 8 \implies k = 4$, making the two lines coincident so every point on the line is a solution.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Without solving for $x$ and $y$ individually, find the value of $x + y$ given that $7x + 5y = 31$ and $5x + 7y = 17$.
step_by_step_solution: Add the two equations directly: $(7x + 5y) + (5x + 7y) = 31 + 17 \implies 12x + 12y = 48$.
Factor out $12$ and divide both sides by $12$: $12(x + y) = 48 \implies x + y = 4$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Prove that for any constants $p$ and $q$, the system $x + y = p$ and $x - y = q$ always has the unique solution $x = \frac{p + q}{2}$ and $y = \frac{p - q}{2}$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Adding gives $2x = p + q \implies x = \frac{p+q}{2}$; subtracting gives $2y = p - q \implies y = \frac{p-q}{2}$
step_by_step_solution: Add the two equations: $(x + y) + (x - y) = p + q \implies 2x = p + q \implies x = \frac{p + q}{2}$.
Subtract the second equation from the first: $(x + y) - (x - y) = p - q \implies 2y = p - q \implies y = \frac{p - q}{2}$.
